client: I've been really struggling since I started college last semester — the workload is just so much more than I expected, and I feel like I'm constantly behind no matter how hard I try. It's gotten to the point where I've basically stopped hanging out with my friends because I feel like I should be studying, but then I just end up sitting alone feeling terrible about everything. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the assignments are still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting — and I notice even in the way you're speaking, there's a kind of urgency and tension that tells me this has been building for a while. You're right that the assignments will still be there, but I wonder if we can look at whether the story you're telling yourself — that you're "constantly behind" no matter what — is fully accurate, or if that belief itself might be adding to the weight you're feeling. Isolating yourself to study more, but then feeling too overwhelmed to actually study, is a really common cycle, and recognizing it is actually a meaningful first step we can work with together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying about the story I'm telling myself, but honestly it doesn't feel like just a story — like, I actually do have three papers due next week and I'm barely halfway through one of them. I guess I can see what you mean about the cycle, because I'll sit down to study and then just spiral into this panicked feeling where I can't focus on anything. But I'm not sure recognizing it really helps when the deadlines are still real and I still feel completely unprepared.
therapist: You're absolutely right that the deadlines are real, and I don't want to dismiss that — and I can hear in your voice a kind of strained, pressured energy, like you're carrying this urgency even as you're trying to think it through with me. What I'm curious about is whether that spiral you described — sitting down and then freezing in panic — is actually costing you more time than it's saving, because the avoidance and the anxiety together might be a bigger obstacle right now than the papers themselves. If we can find a way to interrupt that panic cycle, even slightly, it might actually change what's possible with the time you do have.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually makes some sense to me, like I can see how I'm probably wasting hours just sitting there frozen instead of actually getting anything done. But I guess my worry is that even if I could calm the panic down somehow, I still don't really know how to tackle these papers — it's not just anxiety, I genuinely feel lost about what I'm supposed to be doing. It's like the panic and the not-knowing are all tangled up together and I can't tell where one ends and the other begins.
therapist: The way you just described that — the panic and the not-knowing being tangled together — is actually a really important insight, and I can hear in your voice a kind of strained, almost breathless quality that tells me this feels genuinely overwhelming right now, not just in your thoughts but in your whole system. What you're describing makes a lot of sense, because anxiety has a way of mimicking confusion — when we're flooded with panic, it's nearly impossible to access what we actually do know. So I'm wondering if it might be worth gently separating those two threads: starting with one small, concrete piece of just one paper, not to solve everything, but just to test whether some of the "not-knowing" starts to loosen once the panic has a little less fuel.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to try that, I really do, but even thinking about picking just one small piece feels hard because I don't know which piece to start with and then I'm back to feeling stuck again. It's like every part of the paper feels equally urgent and equally confusing, so trying to choose just makes the panic worse. I guess I'm also a little scared that if I try your suggestion and it doesn't work, I'll feel even more hopeless than I do now.
therapist: That fear of trying and it not working — and ending up feeling worse — is such a vulnerable thing to name, and it tells me how much you're already carrying right now. I notice your voice has a kind of tightness to it, like you're bracing yourself, which makes complete sense given how many times you've probably sat down with good intentions and ended up frozen. What if we took the pressure of "choosing the right starting point" completely off the table, and instead just picked something almost arbitrarily small — like writing one sentence, any sentence, about any part of one paper — not because it's the perfect move, but just to show your nervous system that starting doesn't have to be catastrophic?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: One sentence feels almost too small to matter, like it's not going to make a dent in three papers due next week. But I think part of me is also kind of relieved by the idea, because it doesn't sound as terrifying as sitting down and trying to write the whole thing. I guess I'm just worried I'll write one sentence and then feel proud of myself for like two seconds before the panic about everything else comes crashing back in.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — softly, quickly, like you're thinking out loud and almost afraid to let yourself hope — tells me that small flicker of relief you just described is real and worth paying attention to, even if it feels fragile. You're right that the panic might come back after that one sentence, but here's the CBT reframe: the goal isn't to make the panic disappear, it's to prove to yourself that you can act *despite* it, which actually weakens its grip over time. That two seconds of feeling proud isn't nothing — it's evidence against the story that you're helpless, and we can build on evidence.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think what you're saying about acting despite the panic makes sense in theory, but I'm not sure I fully believe yet that two seconds of feeling okay is actually going to add up to anything. Like, I want to believe it, but I've had moments before where I felt like I was making progress and then the next day I was right back to feeling completely behind and alone. I guess what I'm asking is, how do I keep from just falling back into the same place when the next wave of panic hits?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, with a kind of high, tight energy — tells me this question isn't just intellectual curiosity, it's coming from a real fear of being hurt by hope again, and that makes complete sense given what you've been through. What you're describing is actually one of the most important things we can work on together: not just building momentum, but building a plan for when the wave hits, so it doesn't catch you completely off guard. That might look like identifying one specific thing you'll do *when* the panic returns — not if — so that instead of the wave sweeping you back to square one, you have a small anchor waiting for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of having an anchor, but I honestly don't know what that would even look like for me in that moment — like when the panic hits, my mind just goes completely blank and I can't think of anything helpful to do. And I guess I'm a little skeptical that whatever we come up with in this calm, quiet office is actually going to be accessible to me when I'm alone at midnight staring at a blank document. How do you make something stick when the version of you that needs it most is the one who's least able to remember it?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, with a kind of high, strained pitch — tells me that even asking this question is activating something, like part of you is already in that midnight-panic place just imagining it. You've actually put your finger on something really important in CBT: the anchor has to be so simple and so physical that your thinking brain doesn't need to be online to access it — something like a single word written on a sticky note on your laptop, or one specific physical action like putting your feet flat on the floor and taking one breath. The goal is to make it so small and concrete that the most overwhelmed version of you can still find it, almost on autopilot.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: The sticky note idea is actually something I can picture, which is more than I can say for most things we've talked about today. I think I'd want it to say something really simple, maybe just "one sentence" as a reminder of what you said earlier, so it connects back to something that already felt a little less scary. I'm still not a hundred percent sure it'll work when I'm in that place, but I guess it's at least something I could actually try without it feeling completely overwhelming.
therapist: The fact that you landed on that yourself — "one sentence" in your own handwriting, connected to something that already felt manageable — is genuinely meaningful, and even though your voice still carries a kind of tension and uncertainty, there's something quieter underneath it that wasn't there at the start of our conversation. That skepticism you're holding onto, the "I'm not a hundred percent sure it'll work," is actually healthy — it means you're not setting yourself up for all-or-nothing thinking, just a genuine experiment. And that shift, from "nothing will help" to "here's one small thing I could actually try," is exactly the kind of movement that CBT builds on.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think you're right that something has shifted a little, even though I'm almost hesitant to admit it because I don't want to get my hopes up too much. It's weird, because I came in here pretty convinced that talking wasn't going to change anything, and I still have all the same papers and deadlines waiting for me. But I guess I feel slightly less like I'm drowning in it, which isn't nothing, even if I'm not totally sure what to do with that feeling yet.
therapist: The way you said that — carefully, almost like you were testing whether it was safe to say out loud — tells me that "slightly less like I'm drowning" is actually a bigger shift than you're giving yourself credit for, even if you're protecting yourself from leaning into it too fully. You don't have to know what to do with that feeling yet; you can just let it be true that something moved today, even while the papers are still waiting. That's not false hope — that's real evidence, gathered in this room, that you're not as stuck as you thought you were.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I needed to hear that it counts as evidence, because my brain usually just dismisses any small progress as not being enough. It's still a little hard to fully trust it, because I know I'm going to walk out of here and the loneliness and the panic are probably going to creep back in tonight when I'm sitting alone with those papers. But maybe I'll try writing that sticky note when I get back, just to see if it actually does anything when I need it most.
therapist: There's something that strikes me about this moment — your words are reaching toward something hopeful, but your voice is carrying a lot, fast and tight and loud, like part of you is already bracing for tonight. That tension makes complete sense, and I want you to know that the loneliness and panic creeping back in doesn't erase what happened here today — it just means you'll have a chance to use your anchor for the first time. Writing that sticky note isn't just a practical step; it's you choosing to leave yourself something kind for the version of you who needs it most, and that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
